(FOX26) — California Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, 75 (R), San Diego, is criticizing a Democrat proposal to limit citizen journalism and public scrutiny of taxpayer-funded organizations. AB 2624, which DeMaio has dubbed the “Stop Nick Shirley Act,” argues that it targets independent journalists who use video to expose alleged fraud and abuse in government programs.Nick Shirley is the independent YouTube journalist who brought nationwide attention to alleged daycare fraud in Minnesota and hospice and Medicare fraud in California.Play/PauseVideo Qualityauto640x360, 981kbps854x480, 1641kbps1280x720, 2521kbps1920x1080, 3851kbpsSpeed0.25x0.5xnormal1.5x2xAudio TrackAudio QualityautoSubtitlesopenoffCaptions (CC1)Font sizedefault50%75%100%150%200%300%400%Font styledefaultitalicboldFont familydefaultmonospaced serifproportional serifmonospaced sans serifproportional sans serifcasualcursivesmall capitalFont colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagentaFont opacitydefault100%75%50%25%Character edgedefaultraiseddepresseduniformdrop shadowedCharacter edge colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagentaBackground colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagentaBackground opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0%Window colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagentaWindow opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0%BackReset00:0003:38PlayMutePicture-in-PictureApple AirPlayGoogle CastVRSettingsFullscreenAB 2624ReplaylogoIn the video, Nick Shirley and his team go to various daycare and hospice centers and allege fraud. (TNND)[RELATED] Nick Shirley releases California alleged fraud video on X, says its bigger than MinnesotaSupporters say the bill is meant to protect immigrant-serving organizations from threats, but DeMaio contends its broad language could apply to a wide range of groups.Powered By 00:19/03:3810 Sec 11.9K 1Video of big rig crash on I-5 highlights need for safe distance, defensive driving NextStay At a recent hearing, Assemblyman DeMaio pressed the bill’s author, Mia Bonta, who is the wife of California's Attorney General Rob Bonta.He pointed out provisions of the bill could allow organizations to demand the removal of publicly recorded videos and pursue financial penalties against those who share them online.DeMaio warned the bill could discourage investigative reporting and intimidate journalists and watchdogs documenting potential wrongdoing.[RELATED] Valley assemblywoman finds 197 hospice agencies registered at one LA address“California Democrats are trying to intimidate citizen watchdog journalists and protect waste and fraud happening in far-Left-wing NGOs," said DeMaio. Instead of fixing the fraud problems being uncovered, Sacramento politicians are trying to shut down the people exposing them.He called AB 2624 “an attack on transparency and the First Amendment” and urged it be defeated.Click here to watch the Assembly hearing.Valley Assemblyman David Tangipa also weighed in on the bill. "AB 2624 would expand restrictions on recording inside certain facilities—including organizations that receive taxpayer funding. That means journalists and independent investigators, like Nick Shirley, could face legal penalties simply for documenting what’s happening behind closed doors. Think about that for a second. Courageous and patriotic people trying to expose fraud, abuse, or mismanagement could be legally punished while the people receiving millions of our taxpayer dollars get even less scrutiny, Tangipa said.And who’s backing this bill? Groups like CHIRLA—an organization that has received millions in taxpayer funding while pushing radical open borders immigration policy!Comment with BubblesREAD THE COMMENTS (5)"Now, the same corrupt leftwing NGO's benefiting from your tax dollars are supporting legislation that gives them even less accountability and less transparency," said Tangipa. "This should concern every Californian, no matter your politics. Newsom says 'No' to gas tax pauseby Adjoa AikinsWed, April 22, 2026 at 5:17 PMGov. Gavin Newsom speaks at an Earth Day event in Madera County, where he announced three new California State Parks and addressed questions on state transportation funding, including the gas tax. (California Governor Gavin Newsom)Comment on this story0CommentShare storyShareMADERA COUNTY, Calif. (FOX26) — Governor Gavin Newsom marked Earth Day Wednesday with the announcement of three new California State Parks in the Central Valley, while also drawing a firm line on one of the state’s most debated policy questions, the gas tax.Speaking alongside First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom and state and local leaders, the governor unveiled new park sites in Fresno, Yuba, and Kern counties as part of what officials are calling a historic expansion of California’s park system.The additions include the San Joaquin River Parkway along Fresno’s northern edge, Feather River Park south of Marysville, and the Sunset Migratory Labor Camp near Bakersfield, a historic site dating back to the 1930s.“This is about belonging,” Gov. Newsom said during the event. “These places are about connection, about making sure every Californian has access to nature.”But the press conference also turned briefly to transportation policy, when the governor was asked directly whether he would consider suspending California’s gas tax amid ongoing concerns about fuel prices.“No, nor does Ron DeSantis believe that's appropriate or Donald Trump,” the governor said plainly.He went on to defend the tax, saying it supports critical infrastructure projects across the state.“It’s funding the biggest investments in roads and bridges and infrastructure in California’s history,” He said, pointing to the state’s long-term capital outlay for transportation.The governor also argued that recent price spikes at the pump are tied to broader national and international factors, including federal policy and global energy markets.“The price spikes in this state are directly attributable to the actions of the President of the United States,” he said.Despite the policy exchange, the focus of the event remained on expanding access to public lands. State Parks officials said the new additions are part of a broader effort to bring outdoor spaces closer to underserved communities, particularly in the Central Valley.California State Parks Director Armando Quintero said the expansion builds on a larger strategy to “bring the park system to the inside” of the state, rather than just along its coastal edges.Officials say the new parks are expected to undergo public planning and input before being fully established, with California’s total state park system projected to grow to 283 sites once finalized.Comment with BubblesBE THE FIRST TO
